_doc: Neon Debt's interface as data, owned by the ui-artist. The palette is not copied here: it is read out of the art pipeline's own PALETTE, so a colour changed for the sprites changes for the interface in the same commit. Every key is documented in the skill's templates/ui.json.
_fonts: The faces are OFL and already in the repo; the ui-artist owns which face does what, not the glyphs. VT323 is a pixel face at 28 px; Orbitron at weight 800 is the display face, for the title and the boss's name only.

body.role: every label, every menu, the dialogue

display.role: the title and the boss bar; never a paragraph

_source: Where the interface is drawn in code. Every Color() these files type is measured against the palette by lint.py.
_constants: The generated file the UI code imports instead of typing colours. export.py writes it; nothing edits it by hand.

header: The interface's colours, generated by the ui-artist from ui/ui.json.
Do not edit: change the palette in game/tools/art/pixel.py or the role
A role is what a colour means on screen, not what it looks like: the HP
bar is HP, and if the game's red moves it moves here once. Each comment
below says whether the role takes a palette entry -- the same colours the
sprites are snapped onto -- or holds its own, and why.
constants._aliases: The constant names the code already uses, mapped to the role each one means. The rewire matches a colour by its value; this is the tie-break where the values cluster, which for this game is the five near-blacks (PANEL, DOOR, TITLE_OUTLINE, SCRIM, TITLE_GROUND) that sit inside a few dE of each other.
_roles: A role is what a colour means on screen. Each one either takes a palette entry (`palette`) or holds its own value (`rgb`) with the reason it is not a palette entry.

The names are the ones the code already used, so the rewire is a substitution and not a rename. Where the code typed one name for two colours, the role table picks one and says which and why: that is the whole point of having a table.

The `rgb` roles are the interface's own colours. They are not in the palette because the palette is what rig.py's snap_to_palette votes every baked sprite onto: an interface colour added there would re-snap the art. Whether each one should move to its nearest palette entry instead is the art-director's call; lint.py prints the distance.

TEXT.why: the body text. The code had two COL_TEXT, this one in the six menus and (217,230,247) in the four in-world overlays, dE 3.4 apart; no one could say which screen they were looking at, so one wins.

DIM.why: labels, hints, anything the eye is meant to skip. Eleven files typed it and none disagreed, which is what a role looks like before it has a name.

ACCENT.why: focus, the speaker's name, the active tab, the current room. The code had five names for it: COL_ACCENT, COL_ACTIVE, COL_NAME, COL_CURRENT, COL_SPEAKER.

GOOD.why: an upgrade, a quest done, a stat that went up. Was COL_GOOD and COL_BETTER.

BAD.why: a downgrade or a failure. Was COL_BAD, COL_WORSE, and the title's COL_WARN, which was this colour and not a warning.

WARN.why: a caution the player can still act on, the settings panel's only orange. The title screen called its red COL_WARN as well; that one is BAD.

HP.why: the health bar. Six dE off the palette's red, which is the one snap worth arguing about: the bar is the most looked-at thing on the screen.

HACK.why: a hack that can be cast, against RAM's violet. A hand-lightened violet with no palette step of its own.

SAVE.why: a save point on the map, against ACCENT's current room. A hand-lightened cyan.

ROOM_EDGE.why: the map's room borders, a step lighter than the rooms themselves.

HP_LOW.why: already the palette exactly; the code just retyped it. Also SELECTED.

XP.why: already the palette (dE 0.1). Also the title's COL_NEON.

CREDITS.why: already the palette exactly, typed inline in the HUD.

PANEL.why: the panel ground, matching the theme's stylebox. The code had two: the ending screen's, which matched the theme, and the dialogue box's, 2.1 dE lighter for no reason anyone wrote down.

ROOM.why: the map's rooms; 1.5 dE off, under the just-noticeable difference, so it snaps.

DOOR.why: the map's doors; 2.1 dE off, so it snaps.

roles._theme: Below: the roles the theme's styleboxes take. They were only ever in theme.json, which is how the buttons ended up a shade the rest of the interface had never heard of.

BUTTON.why: a button at rest; 2.3 dE off, so it snaps.

BUTTON_HOVER.why: a button under the cursor or the focus; 1.5 dE off, so it snaps.

SLIDER_TRACK.why: the groove a slider runs in. Two point seven dE from bg2, just over the line, and snapping it there would make a track and a hovered button the same colour, which they are not.

FOCUS.why: the focus ring and the hovered label; already the palette (dE 0.1).

roles._scene: Below: colours that are scene art rather than interface chrome. They were typed inline, which is why nothing could find them; they are roles because a title screen's sky is as much a decision as a label's grey.

VIGNETTE.why: the damage flash over the whole screen. A deep red with no palette step; the palette's red_d is 22 dE away and reads brown behind a HUD.

TITLE_OUTLINE.why: the outline behind the title's 132 px letters. Colder than bg0 by 3.5 dE so the neon sits off the sky rather than on it.

SKYLINE_FAR.why: the far parallax skyline. The pair with SKYLINE_NEAR is the depth: change one and the distance changes.

RAIN.why: the rain sheet on the title, drawn at alpha 0.35.

SCRIM.why: the dim over the title behind its menu, at alpha 0.35. Three dE under void and the only true black in the game.

TITLE_GROUND.why: the title's ground band; half a dE from void, so it snaps.

_theme_roles: Which role each colour in theme.json takes. `export.py --theme` writes those values into the theme, keeping each one's alpha, so the theme and the code cannot hold two versions of the same colour. A theme colour missing from this map is a finding: it is a colour with no meaning attached.
_sprites: The screen furniture. The grids are in ui/sprites.py; this block is what the engine needs to know about each one. `margins` are the nine-patch margins in texture px (art px x scale). `used_by` is a note, checked by the lint: a frame no source file names is dead art.
_screens: Every screen the interface draws, its file, and the budget it may take of the design resolution. `over` names the room shot it is judged on: a HUD is judged over the room it never leaves, a menu over the room it pauses.

`rect` is the panel's rectangle as fractions of the screen [left, top, right, bottom], read off the engine's own anchors rather than guessed, with the arithmetic in the note beside it. A screen with no rect is judged over the whole shot, which is right for a menu that covers the room.

Where the code positions by offset instead of anchor, the fraction is that offset over the design resolution: the HUD's box sits at (28, 22) and a bar row is a 58 px label plus 10 separation plus a 228 px frame, so 296 x 22 a row, three rows and the pips at separation 6 -> about 296 x 130 from (28, 22), which over 1920 x 1080 is the rect below.

hud.note: never leaves the screen; the tightest budget in the game

debug.note: a developer readout, never shipped to a player; its colours are not the game's

_shots: The two shots the interface is judged over: the darkest the game gets and the brightest. A `shot` is a png already taken; a `room` is shot fresh through the level-artist's runner (mock.py --room), which is the better source once the district is dressed.

These two were picked by measuring, not by eye: level-artist/scripts/ref_stats.py over every shot in game/tools/art/work/scale/ on 2026-09-16. The roof is 96% dark with 20% of its lit pixels warm, the only sodium in the set; shot_b is the brightest real room at 52% dark and 15% bright. The all-dark lamp renders and the contact sheets in that folder are not rooms and were not eligible.

dark.note: the rooftop: 96% dark, 20% warm; the darkest room a player stands in

bright.note: 52% dark, 15% bright; the brightest real room in the set

_contrast: The floors, as WCAG contrast ratios, measured against the panel as it is drawn: a stylebox at alpha 0.94 over a room is not the colour in the file.

`critical` is text that carries a number the player acts on, held to 7:1. A bar is not text and is not on this list: it is a block of colour the size of a thumb, and it is judged against its own track and against the room, not against a paragraph's floor. HP at 6.4:1 over the panel reads at a glance; the same ratio under a sentence would not.
_allow: Colours the lint does not measure against the palette: pure black and white are structural (a fade, a mask, a modulate), not a choice of shade.
